result:
The proposed answer of 1/3 is not correct. The solution only asserts "symmetry and integral geometry" and never computes anything, so I checked the value for plausibility.

A line through two interior points meets the hexagon's boundary in exactly two points, so it can cross at most one pair of opposite edges. The three events are therefore mutually exclusive, and the answer is 3 times the probability for one specific pair.

The 1/3 figure is too small for two reasons:
- Any line through the center of the hexagon meets the boundary at two opposite points, so it crosses a pair of opposite edges (or passes through opposite vertices, which has probability zero).
- Lines that cross only non-opposite edges cut off a corner of the hexagon. Such chords are short, so they carry little weight when the two points are chosen at random inside the hexagon. Long chords between opposite sides carry most of the weight.

Both points suggest the true probability is well above 1/3, probably around 0.7. I did not compute the exact value.

VERDICT: REJECT
